extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners learning persuasion (marketers, salespeople, communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply Robert Cialdini’s six principles of persuasion (reciprocity, scarcity, authority, commitment/consistency, consensus/social proof, liking) to real-world persuasive scenarios such as sales and marketing. The page explains each principle and gives examples and application prompts for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objective: Explain the six principles of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the six principles of persuasion identified by Cialdini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to name and describe each of Cialdini’s six principles (reciprocity, scarcity, authority, commitment and consistency, consensus/social proof, liking) and understand how they operate cross-culturally. No scoring rubric given; this functions as a learning outcome to guide comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objective: Apply Cialdini’s principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Cialdini’s principles to a real life persuasive scenario.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are expected to recognize and analyze real-world examples (e.g., a sales interaction) to identify which principles are being used and how they influenced behavior. The application exercise asks learners to deconstruct an upsell/regretful purchase and map the salesperson’s tactics to the principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: I scratch your back; you scratch mine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocity means when you give something to somebody, they feel obligated to give something back, even if only by saying 'thank you.' In customer service, going out of your way to meet a customer's need appeals to reciprocity and builds trust and loyalty, increasing likelihood of purchase. Reciprocity builds relationships and creates a social obligation motivating the receiver to follow social norms and give back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: People are naturally attracted to the rare and exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scarcity is the perception of a dwindling supply of a limited and valuable product; convincing people they must act now (or risk losing the opportunity) motivates action. In sales, highlighting what customers stand to lose (limited stock, exclusivity) can move them from contemplation to purchase. The key is creating a believable perception of limited availability or exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing experts or authoritative sources increases credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrasing such as 'According to researchers...' makes statements sound more true because authority builds trust. Endorsements or expert knowledge carry credibility that vested-interest sources cannot. Salespeople can be more effective by demonstrating product/field knowledge and referencing experts or research; this requires doing extra homework beyond product manuals. The principle involves borrowing credibility from recognized experts or expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Commitment and Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Once people commit, they feel obligated to follow through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public or written commitments increase the pressure to honor one’s word (e.g., announcing plans on social media). In sales, getting a customer to make a small commitment — signing up for a store card or rewards program — increases the likelihood of consistent follow-through with related purchases. The mechanism is that visible commitments make behaviors feel 'official' and motivate consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Consensus / Social Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: People look to others' behavior or reviews when deciding what to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social proof operates when people trust first-person testimonials or the apparent unanimity of many endorsements; the 'herd mentality' simplifies decision-making when credible information is lacking. Online reviews and numerous positive testimonials signal that a product is good, encouraging others to follow. The principle is especially powerful when many people appear to agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: We are more likely to comply with requests from people we like or identify with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People buy from those they like, find attractive, or see as similar. Perceived similarity, relatability, or expressed liking by a salesperson can trigger reciprocity and increase compliance. Attractiveness may convey implicit authority; sharing personal stories of solving the same problem creates identification and increases persuasion ('this person and I are similar... they solved it by doing X, so I can too').
